1:
Ellicott marks the turn: the charges so far had concerned Christian life among Christians, but there was a great life outside that little world. Why the reminder was needed in Crete draws four explanations. Ellicott gives the political history: the island had been a century and a quarter under Roman rule after a democratic government, historians dwelt on the turbulent spirit of its people, and a large Jewish population was always impatient of a foreign yoke. Gill supplies the reputation rather than the history: the Romans did not distinguish Christians from Jews, and the Jews were reckoned turbulent and seditious, partly through principles about withholding tribute from Caesar and partly through the insurrections of Judas of Galilee and Theudas. Clarke adds a fragment from a lexicographer about Cretans who, fearing punishment, stirred up the populace by exhorting them to preserve their ancestral liberty — then draws the line it invites: to be jealous of our civil rights is praiseworthy, but to raise a public tumult to avoid merited chastisement under pretense that those privileges are in danger is not the part of patriots but insurgents. Calvin looks past Crete to the constant difficulty: the apostles had great trouble keeping the common people subject, since we are all by nature desirous of power and no one willingly is subject to another; and nearly all the powers of the world being then opposed to Christ, men thought them unworthy of honour.

Two smaller points are agreed on. Gill and Ellicott both guard the first noun against a misreading: it does not mean angels, though it is sometimes so used, but men in high places — which is why Ellicott prefers rulers and authorities. Robertson notices a remarkable double asyndeton, with no conjunction between either pair. Where they part is on what readiness to every good work covers. Henry reports that some refer it to works required by magistrates, and grants this is included and perhaps first intended, but refuses to have it restrained there: the precept regards doing good in all kinds and on every occasion, and mere harmlessness or good meanings are not enough without good works. Calvin leans the other way, applying it to what precedes, as if Paul had said that all who do not refuse to lead a good and virtuous life will cheerfully yield obedience to magistrates — though if any prefer to read it without relation to the context, he has no objection. His reason is strong: since magistrates were appointed for the preservation of mankind, he who desires them removed or shakes off their yoke is an enemy of equity and justice, and devoid of all humanity.

The command to speak evil of no man produces the most careful writing here. Barnes takes the verb in its strong sense of blaspheming, then works out what it permits, since we may be called to state what we know of a man's character and may have to say things not in his favour. He sets conditions: never for the purpose of injury or with pleasure taken in it; no improper colouring, no circumstance exaggerated; never any attempt to charge bad motives on him, for we know not what his motives were; and every palliating circumstance stated. We should show that we would rather find him a good man than a bad one, even if the result were that we had been mistaken — better that we should have been mistaken than that he should be a bad man. Ellicott hears the charge as breathing the spirit of Christ, who when he was reviled reviled not again, and supplies the historical vindication, quoting the boast that when Julian asked Christians to sacrifice to the gods they sternly refused, but when he summoned them to fight for the empire they rushed to the front — distinguishing their Eternal Lord from their earthly ruler, and yet obeying the latter.
3:
How far the apostle includes himself divides them, and each answer changes the tone of the verse. Barnes denies the narrow reading, naming the commentator who confined it to Paul and objecting that some things mentioned here were probably not true of him before his conversion: Paul is stating why those Titus preached to should be urged to good lives, namely that those now Christians were formerly wicked and disorderly, and the gospel effectual in their case might be so in others. Clarke has no doubt Paul felt he could include himself, and explains how a man might belong in such a list while walking blameless according to the letter of the law: the manner in which he persecuted the Christians, to whose charge he could lay not one moral evil, is sufficient proof that his heart was in great estrangement from God and from justice and compassion. Gill includes him too, noting he had a zeal for God and yet stood in the catalogue. Ellicott makes it a rhetorical act rather than a biographical claim, these being the lusts of the people with whom for the moment the Apostle was classing himself; and he presses the force it would have on the man delivering it, since Titus was of a Gentile family and probably nurtured in idolatry, so that the argument would be repeated with touching earnestness to the Cretan assembly.

The purpose of the retrospect is agreed, and stated most fully by Barnes and Ellicott. Barnes turns it into a rule for preachers: they were not to be proud or arrogant but to remember they had been in the same condition as those they exhorted, and that what they had which was superior they owed to grace and not native goodness — he will exhort the wicked most effectually who remembers that his own former life was wicked. He extends it beyond the pulpit: when a Christian is tempted to unkind thoughts or words, nothing is more appropriate than to reflect on his own past life. Ellicott puts it as a question the Cretans must answer: shall we, once like them, now refuse all sympathy to these poor souls still left in ignorance and sin? Gill gives it from the other end, that nothing has a greater tendency to promote humility and check pride than to reflect on what we once were; and the same grace which made a difference in us could make one in these also, in God's own time.

On the individual words the readings diverge. Barnes takes deceived as something done to us, by the great enemy, by false teachers, by our own hearts and by the flattery of others, and adds that it is characteristic of man to walk amidst constant though changing illusions. Ellicott prefers going astray, wandering from the narrow road that leads to life, and Clarke the same, erring in consequence of our ignorance and, because of our unbelief, not choosing to know the way — there are none so blind, he says, as those who will not see, and such persons are proof against conviction. Robertson notes that the participle is passive though the middle is possible — precisely the ambiguity the others resolve in opposite directions. Clarke reserves his strongest complaint for the fourth verse, regretting that an attribute of the divine nature has been entirely lost by a paraphrastical translation: the word is philanthropy, a character God here gives himself, and while human nature exists it must remain a character of the divine nature. God loved man when the idea was formed in his own infinite mind, and when man fell the same love devised his redemption, so that God the Saviour flows from God the Philanthropist. Barnes makes the same point more briefly, that the Greek word is the love of man and the whole plan of salvation was founded on it.
5:
All agree that works are excluded and part company over how. Ellicott is careful about what the denial does not say: it does not assert that such works were ever done and found insufficient, only that to win salvation such must be done — and sad experience has shown the impossibility of any of us, even the holiest, doing the works of a purely righteous man for one day. Clarke argues from the catalogue just given: those who were foolish and deceived and serving divers lusts could have no works of righteousness to plead, so if saved at all it must be by mercy. Barnes makes it a fundamental principle that the good works of men come in for no share in the justification of the soul, adding that after all our tears and prayers and good deeds it remains a mere favour, which God might justly withhold with no blame attaching to him.

The washing of regeneration divides them three ways, and each knows he contradicts somebody. Barnes takes the noun to mean a bath rather than a laver, allows it would naturally be understood of baptism, then draws the line hard: baptism is the emblem, not the means, of purifying the soul. It is nowhere taught in the New Testament that baptism is regeneration; the word occurs only here and in one place where it indubitably does not refer to baptism; its correlatives are applied only to the moral change produced by the Spirit; and the usage leaves the impression that the only change needful is that which accompanies a regular baptism — on almost no point, he says, has so much injury been done in the church. He reads the next clause as Paul's own guard against the error, since without the renewing of the Holy Ghost the former would be unmeaning. Clarke says undoubtedly the apostle means baptism, then holds both ends at once: it is only a sign and should never be separated from the thing signified, but it is a rite commanded by God and the thing signified should never be expected without it — baptism changes nothing, and they who think baptism to be regeneration neither know the Scriptures nor the power of God. Ellicott goes furthest. The laver can only signify the baptismal font, and by means of it God has put us into a state of salvation: baptism is the means through which we receive the saving grace of Christ, and in its laver we are born again. But he takes baptism in its completion, the outward sign accompanied by inward grace, requiring repentance and faith in one come to years of understanding, and in infants the same profession made by sureties and assented to afterwards.

The outpouring produces a smaller but flatter contradiction. Robertson refers it to the great Pentecost as foretold by the prophet; Barnes says there is no particular allusion to Pentecost here, the sense being that the Spirit has been imparted richly to all converted at any time or place. Clarke hears baptism still in the verb, and makes the manner do the work: since the water was sometimes only sprinkled, the heavenly gift was poured not in drops but richly. Ellicott divides the verse among the three Persons — the Father pours out the Spirit, the Son's atonement makes it possible, the Spirit builds up the new life — and notes that Saviour, given to the Father a verse earlier, is here given to the Son: the Father is architect of our salvation, the Son its builder. Gill turns to the justification, an act of God's gracious will conceived from eternity and pronounced on Christ at his resurrection, merely declared in regeneration — which justifies no one but makes the justified appear to be such. Cyril, quoting the verse, prays that the Father of glory would give a spirit of wisdom and revelation.
8:
What the good works are is disputed at once, and the two answers pull opposite ways. Chrysostom narrows it: having considered the exceeding love of God for man, Paul thence exhorts to almsgiving, and not slightly but that they may be careful to maintain it — succouring the injured not only with money but by patronage and protection, defending widows and orphans, affording refuge to all that are afflicted, for this is to maintain good works. He grants that what has been said applies to humility and to every other virtue, but the charge itself he takes as charitable. Barnes widens what Chrysostom narrows: the good works refer not merely to acts of benevolence and charity but to all that is upright and good, an honest and holy life; and the doctrines were no matters of speculation but were fitted to promote human happiness, and so should be constantly taught. Clarke enumerates what these things are — the ruined state of man, the goodness of God which devised his salvation, its manifestation in the incarnation, the justification received through his blood, the mission of the Spirit, the hope of the resurrection, the necessity of obedience — all of which Paul wills Titus to press continually.

The foolish questions are read against the local situation. Henry sets them against Crete and the many judaizers there, distinguishing needful questions that make for useful knowledge from idle enquiries tending neither to God's glory nor the edification of men, which may have a show of wisdom but are vain. On the genealogies he canvasses two possibilities, those of the gods the heathen poets made such noise about, or rather those the Jews were curious in; and he allows some enquiry into the latter is lawful, to see the fulfilling of the scriptures in the descent of the Messiah, while condemning what serves pomp only and feeds vanity in a long pedigree — the more so since the distinction of families and tribes had been taken away, so that to pursue them is to build again a policy now abolished. Chrysostom guesses at the same target, that Paul glances at the Jews who, priding themselves on having Abraham for their forefather, neglected their own part; such things are foolish because it is the part of folly to confide in things unprofitable.

The command to reject a heretic raises a difficulty Chrysostom alone states and answers: how does Paul elsewhere say God may peradventure give them repentance, and here that such a man is to be rejected after the first and second admonition? In the former, he replies, Paul speaks of correcting those of whom he had hope, who had simply made opposition; but when a man is perverted and predetermined not to change his mind, and is known and manifest to all, why labour in vain, sowing upon a rock, when the same honourable toil might be spent on one's own people? On the last phrase the two explanations differ in mechanism. Chrysostom makes it evidential: he cannot say that no one told him or admonished him, and since after admonition he continues the same, he is self-condemned. Henry makes it an act: such men inflict on themselves the punishment the governors of the church should inflict, throwing themselves out of her communion. Henry adds the image that gives the word its weight, a building so ruined as to make it difficult if not impossible to raise up again, and locates the cause where it stings: not so much a defect of judgment as a perverseness of the will, through pride or ambition or self-willedness. Yet he is careful on both sides: real heresy is not lightly to be charged upon any though greatly to be taken heed of by all, and pains and patience must be used, the church's means even with heretics being persuasive and rational.
10:
What a heretic is draws four answers, and the word occurs only here in the New Testament. Barnes rests on that and on the related noun, elsewhere rendered sect: the true notion is one who promotes a sect or party, the man who makes divisions in a church instead of promoting unity. Such a man may divide over doctrine or a custom or a rite, making some unimportant matter a ground of distinction and endeavouring to get up a new organization; and such a man, by scriptural usage, is a heretic, not merely one who holds a doctrine different from what is regarded as orthodoxy. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by the same route, noting that in the two other Pauline uses the word does not signify doctrinal error, that sense belonging to later times; and he reconstructs the man, dissatisfied with the discipline Titus had introduced and not improbably considering himself slighted, who withdrew and gathered other discontented spirits into a rival Church — adding that even where no erroneous teaching is present at first, such communities tend ever more to distinguish their teaching from the body they left. Gill gives both senses without choosing, one who prefers his own opinion to the churches' and forms a party, or one who takes away a fundamental doctrine touching the Trinity or the person of Christ; and he distinguishes the terms, that every schismatic may not be a heretic, but every heretic is a schismatic. Clarke identifies him historically instead: here it means one who maintains Judaism against Christianity, or insists on the necessity of circumcision in order to be saved.

On what rejection permits they converge, and two raise the stakes to say so. Barnes sets out the limits in order. The utmost allowed is mere exclusion, and we may not follow the offender with injury; we are not authorized to oppose a man for his mere private opinions; it is not made right to deliver him to the secular arm, or to harm him in body, soul, property or reputation, and no power is given to torture him on the rack or bind him to the stake; we may decline to recognise him as a brother or admit him to office, and beyond this there is no right to go, since he has a right to his own opinion still so far as we are concerned. Clarke asks it more bluntly — if he has shut his heart against conviction, then burn him alive? No: even if demonstrably a heretic and a disturber of the Church's peace, God gives no man any other authority over him but to shun him, doing him no harm in body, soul, character or substance, holding no communion with him, but leaving him to God. Ellicott renders the verb shun or avoid, so that after being exhorted once and twice the contumacious man was left simply to his own devices.

The last phrase divides them again on mechanism. Ellicott takes the strong verb literally, that the man has been turned inside out, and finds the self-condemnation in this, that after being warned once and again he is without the excuse of ignorance, so that his stirring up of party-feeling publicly convicts him of the very wrong he professes to condemn. Clarke locates it in motive, referring it to the Judaizing teacher who maintained his party for filthy lucre's sake and was conscious of his own insincerity, proclaiming his system not from a love of truth but from a desire to get his livelihood — and he turns it on his own age, that were the Church in all countries strictly scrutinized, multitudes of heretics of this kind would be found. Ellicott also explains why the man is unnamed: partly from a loving hope that Titus would win him, partly because the letter was public instruction to many a church besides Crete's.
12:
The closing instructions raise a question about the letter itself. Barnes supposes it was at Nicopolis, probably, that this epistle was written. Clarke and Wesley both prove otherwise from one word: the apostle says he has determined to winter THERE, not here, so he was not yet arrived — Clarke adding that it was probably late in the autumn, Wesley concluding that the letter was not written from thence. On which Nicopolis was meant they converge. Clarke names the city of Epirus near Actium, which Augustus built to commemorate his victory over Mark Antony, and sets aside another of the same name in Thrace; Ellicott lists three, in Cilicia, Thrace and Epirus, and judges the one in Epirus most likely, named from the battle as the City of Victory. Wesley adds a caution the others do not: the subscription at the end of the epistle should not be trusted, none of those subscriptions being of any authority. Ellicott reads the recall as a reminder that Titus is only temporary ruler of the Cretan Church, and Wesley says the same of his office: he was properly an evangelist, who by the nature of that office had no fixed residence but presided over elders wherever he travelled.

The names then draw out what is known and what is not. Of Artemas all say the same, that he is mentioned nowhere else and nothing more is known, though tradition makes him afterwards a bishop. On Zenas the question is what kind of lawyer he was. Ellicott thinks the law he was expert in more likely that of Moses than Roman jurisprudence; Gill agrees, since among the Jews a lawyer and a scribe were one, though one version calls him a scribe of the city, which looks like a civil office; Barnes agrees he belonged to the class qualified to expound the Jewish laws, and is careful that it does not mean he practised law in the modern sense. Clarke alone declines to guess, saying that whether he was Jewish or Roman or Greek we cannot tell. On Apollos, Ellicott is fullest: an Alexandrian scholar converted by Priscilla and Aquila, who might have rivalled or superseded Paul in authority over the churches of the Mediterranean seaboard but resolutely declined, and whom Paul treated as an equal power, classing him with Peter and himself. He reports Luther's suggestion that Apollos wrote the epistle to the Hebrews, disputed as far back as Origen, and notes what nobody else does: the three friends named here, in almost the last letter Paul wrote, all bear names derived from heathen deities.

On the practical charge the voices differ over how narrow it is. Clarke explains the arrangement asked for, that the churches through which these evangelists passed bore their expenses from one to the next. Barnes reads it as hospitality, that they should meet good treatment in Crete and not be embarrassed for want of what was needful. Then comes the last verse, where the margin offers profess honest trades. Barnes allows the Greek will admit or include that, but sees no reason the direction should have peculiar reference to trades, wishing rather that Christians generally be characterized by good works of all kinds. Gill holds both together: an honest employment is a good work and ought to be learnt in order to be followed; and he quotes the saying that he who does not teach his son a trade might as well teach him to steal, the Jewish doctors being brought up to trades as Paul was, though he had an education under Gamaliel. He lists the uses it serves — the good of a man's self, the supply of his family, the assistance of others in need, and the relief of poor saints. Henry states the principle: Christianity is not a fruitless profession, and its professors must be doing good as well as keeping from evil.
